Nova Liu on translating a manual anti-crawler investigation into a reusable Diana Skill — and the small rules that made it work.

Business Security Anti-Crawler Team Interview with Nova.liu

The story

Facing more than 10,000 daily grid curves, Nova.liu needed a faster, more reliable way to investigate fraud. He had conversations with Diana and turned complex SQL and manual verification into guided natural-language workflows.

By continually refining rules, data routing and feedback, the team standardized analysis and reduced each investigation from hours to seconds.

Nova.liu shares the thinking behind the team’s 14-step SOP Skill.

Diana asks

Can you describe your daily work?

Nova.liu: My team works on business security — detecting crawler and scraping behavior on the platform and designing counter-strategies against it. We focus on two key competitive markets, Taiwan and SEA (mainly Indonesia), and look at over ten thousand grid traffic curves every day.

“Now I just need to prompt one command to get a structured report in seconds.”

— Nova.liu

Diana asks

Sounds like heavy work. Would you mind sharing the full process of identifying a suspicious case before using Diana? How long would it take?

Nova.liu: Before Diana, everything was manual SQL on Data Studio. For each candidate, I’d write separate queries and run them one by one. The crawler flag comes from anomalies clustering across two or more dimensions at once, and the judgement was entirely human.

I would then manually narrow 10,000 grids to under 100 suspicious ones, then do a deep-dive analysis. Every manual SQL segment could easily take hours for a single investigation.

 

Diana asks

How did you start using Diana to support your daily work?

Nova.liu: It wasn’t a single first attempt. At first, Diana was just reformatting the SOP framework we provided and following it during case analysis. I wasn’t satisfied — but I found that just talking to Diana gets you far.

So I provided our Python code, SQL, and judgment criteria and said, “Learn this logic.” Every time it messed up, I made a quick rule instead of touching the main SOP. Eventually, all those small rules grew into the official 14-step SOP Skill we use today.

Now I just need to prompt one command to get a structured report in seconds.

Figure 1. Creating a Skill in chat — describe what you need, and the Skill Builder returns an editable draft card.

Did you know?

3 ways to create a new Skill:

  1. Describe it in chat — just say “Create a skill,” and the Skill Builder walks you through it, ending with an editable draft card.
  2. Upload a document — drop in a .md, .pdf, or .docx, and the LLM extracts the skill fields for you.
  3. Build from chat history — Diana notices when a session is worth keeping (2+ tools used, a clear analysis goal, reusable parameters) and proactively asks: “Want to save this analysis as a Skill?”
 

Diana asks

You keep mentioning this 14-step SOP. Can you walk us through what those 14 steps actually cover? What is Diana doing when you fire off that one command?

Nova.liu: The process starts by narrowing 10,000 traffic grids down to the high-frequency buckets worth investigating, then builds the attacker profile across different risk signals. From there, it checks which existing strategies are catching or missing the case, cross-references against known cases, and finally figures out what they’re actually scraping.

Figure 2. The 14-step SOP workflow turns one natural-language command into a structured anti-crawler analysis report.

Did you know?

Your report has these features:

  1. Dashboard-like or PPT-like HTML report — ask Diana or use a Skill to create editable and downloadable reports.
  2. Share to a SeaTalk group — add teammates or user groups as viewers, open viewing to everyone on the Topic, or deliver it to a SeaTalk group — @ someone in the group and they get view access automatically.
  3. Schedule run by a Skill — the report arrives through SeaTalk or email on schedule, even as screenshots readable right in the message — no link-clicking needed.
  4. Keep digging in analysis — quote a report in chat or hit “Continue in Chat” to follow up on any finding where the analysis left off.

Figure 3. From chat to report in one message — say “Turn this into an HTML report,” and the finished report opens in the viewer, ready to edit, download, or share.

“Add small rules to cover the new case — don’t rewrite the core framework.”

Diana asks

From your experience, is there any advice for other Diana users on how to make it actually work for their own workflows?

Nova.liu: There are four tips I can give:

  1. 01Add rules instead of rewriting the core SOP. When business changes, don’t rewrite the core framework. Add small rules to cover the new case.
  2. 02Automate data-source routing. When our sources grew from two tables to three, I just told Diana: “If the query comes back empty, switch to the other table.” Now it picks the right table on its own.
  3. 03Save experience into rules. Judgement built by our team over years is saved as Topic rules, so I never re-explain it in every chat.
  4. 04Correct Diana bluntly to train edge cases. When Diana gets it wrong, I say exactly what’s wrong. Every correction becomes a new rule.
